Arabic يخفي translates 'conceal or hide' correctly — the defect is entirely on the English side.

en_definition: a person who does not talk
expected: a stupid person; also a model of a human figure (a shop or crash-test ___), or a fake copy of something
note: Clear case of the failure mode being hunted. 'A person who does not talk' is the archaic — and now offensive — mute sense; no ordinary speaker reaches for it. The everyday senses are 'idiot', 'mannequin/model', 'fake', and in British English a baby's pacifier. Arabic أبكم ('mute') translates the bad definition correctly, so this is an upstream sense-selection defect, not a translation one.

en_definition: preliminary drawing for later elaboration
note: Rough preliminary drawing is the main sense. Arabic رسم تخطيطي leans 'schematic/diagram'; رسم أولي or رسم مبدئي would carry 'preliminary for later elaboration' more exactly. Minor.

en_definition: spectators at a golf or tennis match
expected: a room or building where works of art are shown
note: Textbook displaced sense — 'spectators at a golf or tennis match' is genuine but almost nobody's first meaning, and a learner would never recover the word from it. The Arabic معرض gives the art-gallery sense, so it does not translate the English as written; fix the English and the Arabic becomes correct.

en_definition: make certain of
note: Clean card. يضمن matches 'make certain of'.

en_definition: occurring among members of a family usually by heredity
expected: relating to genes or to heredity
note: This is the narrow 'hereditary, runs in the family' sense. The everyday adjective is the broader one a learner meets in 'genetic code', 'genetic material', 'genetic engineering', 'genetic testing' — none of which are about families. Recognisable via 'heredity', so secondary not rare. وراثي is the exact equivalent of 'hereditary' and matches the definition as given.

en_definition: motion of hands or body to emphasize or help to express a thought or feeling
note: Everyday sense, clear card. Arabic إيماءة matches.

en_definition: a failure to perform some promised act or obligation
note: Breach of contract/duty/trust is the commonest modern use, and this definition covers it. The physical 'gap in a wall/hull' sense is the runner-up, not the displaced primary. خرق is the standard collocate (خرق القانون).

en_definition: a vehicle that can fly
note: Commonest sense, though 'a vehicle that can fly' is thin for rank 4049; 'a machine that flies, such as a plane or helicopter' would recognise better. Arabic طائرة literally 'flying [thing]' and matches, but in practice reads as 'aeroplane', slightly narrower than aircraft.

en_definition: United States philosopher (1876-1957)
expected: a common English surname and given name; as a common noun, a cider-like drink made from pears
note: Defining 'perry' as Ralph Barton Perry, a US philosopher nobody outside philosophy has heard of, teaches a learner something they will never use. The rank almost certainly comes from the surname/given name in ordinary text (Perry Mason, Katy Perry, Matthew Perry), not from the philosopher, and the drink sense is itself uncommon. Strong candidate for removal from the deck rather than redefinition. Arabic is a bare transliteration and conveys none of the definition.

en_definition: an auxiliary activity
expected: an activity you do regularly for pleasure in your free time
note: 'An auxiliary activity' is the right sense buried in an opaque gloss — it points more at 'sideline' or 'side job' than at hobby, and no learner recovers the word from it. Arabic هواية is the correct everyday equivalent, so the Arabic card is actually better than the English one; marking it faithful because it lands on the intended sense.

en_definition: insane and believed to be affected by the phases of the moon
expected: wildly foolish or crazy
note: The 'affected by the phases of the moon' clause is the archaic/etymological component (WordNet's moonstruck synset). A learner keeps 'insane' but also acquires a false belief about what the word asserts. Arabic مجنون translates 'insane' and simply omits the moon clause — an omission, not a contradiction.

en_definition: move away from a place into another direction
note: Correct 'leave' sense, but the wording is unidiomatic — 'into another direction' is not English. Suggested rewrite: 'to leave a place, especially to start a journey'. Arabic غادر is exact.

en_definition: the circulating life energy that in Chinese philosophy is thought to be inherent in all things; in traditional Chinese medicine the balance of negative and positive forms in the body is believed to be essential for good health
note: The life-energy sense is the one an English speaker meets (tai chi, chi energy), ahead of the Greek letter, so the sense choice is right — but the definition is an encyclopedia paragraph, not a card. Something like 'life energy that flows through the body, in Chinese thought' would do. Arabic خِي is a bare transliteration that carries none of the definition, and mis-transliterates: خ is kh, not ch. Standard renderings are تشي, or الطاقة الحيوية for the concept.

en_definition: a long walk usually for exercise or pleasure
note: Main sense, correctly stated. Arabic نزهة سيرًا على الأقدام is accurate; نزهة connotes a leisurely outing more than a long walk, so رحلة سيرًا على الأقدام would be a touch closer.

en_definition: marked by extreme and violent energy
expected: extremely angry
note: 'Marked by extreme and violent energy' is the 'furious pace / furious storm' sense; the everyday sense is rage. Note the Arabic غاضب جدًا ('very angry') gives the good sense, so it does NOT translate the definition as written — the English is the upstream defect here, and fixing the English would make the Arabic correct.

en_definition: Scottish insurgent who led the resistance to Edward I; in 1297 he gained control of Scotland briefly until Edward invaded Scotland again and defeated Wallace and subsequently executed him (1270-1305)
expected: a Scottish surname, also used as a first name
note: A biography of William Wallace (1270-1305) as a vocabulary card. At this rank the token is overwhelmingly a character's surname in dialogue, not the medieval Scottish rebel; a learner learns a 13th-century history footnote and still cannot use the word. The real fix is upstream: proper nouns like this probably should not be cards at all. Arabic والاس is the correct transliteration of the name, but it renders only the name, none of the biography — the defect here is English-side, not translation-side.

en_definition: an enclosed passageway; rooms usually open onto it
note: English sense is right. Arabic رواق is primarily a portico/arcade/colonnade — an open structure, which contradicts 'enclosed' in the definition. ممر is the unambiguous word for a corridor.

en_definition: a state in the United States in the central Pacific on the Hawaiian Islands
note: Only sense that matters. Arabic is a transliteration of the proper name, which is the correct treatment — nothing to translate.

en_definition: a secret store of valuables or money
note: The ordinary noun sense (a stash of cash), plainly worded. مخبأ leans to 'hiding place' rather than the goods hidden there, a small shift but close enough to the definition as given.

en_definition: a native or inhabitant of Egypt
note: Correct and the only ordinary noun sense; مِصْرِيّ matches.

en_definition: a Russian river in Siberia; flows northward into the Laptev Sea
expected: a woman's given name (also a large river in Siberia)
note: A proper noun that reached the frequency list almost entirely as a personal name in dialogue corpora; the card defines the Siberian river instead. Genuine but useless to a learner, and arguably the entry should be dropped from the deck rather than redefined — same class of defect as 'hooker' in this batch.

en_definition: put in effect
expected: to carry out or achieve something promised, required or hoped for ('___ a promise', '___ a dream')
note: 'Put in effect' points at the right general sense (carry out) but reads as 'implement a policy' and drops the objects that actually collocate: a promise, a duty, a requirement, a dream. The Arabic أَوْفَى is specifically 'kept/honoured a promise' — a reasonable gloss of the headword but not of 'put in effect' (which would be يُنفِّذ). So the Arabic is closer to the right sense than the English definition is.

en_definition: the main organ of photosynthesis and transpiration in higher plants
note: Right sense, but botanical phrasing ("photosynthesis and transpiration in higher plants") makes recognition harder than it should be; "a flat green part growing from the stem of a plant" would serve. Arabic وَرَقَة is the ordinary word and matches the sense.

en_definition: a sudden very loud noise
expected: the sound of hands struck together; a burst of applause
note: 'A sudden very loud noise' is the thunderclap sense — real and common in the collocation 'a clap of thunder', but not what a learner meets first. Note the mismatch this creates: the Arabic تَصْفِيق means clapping/applause, i.e. the sense the English definition does NOT give, so English and Arabic sides of this card disagree.

en_definition: pleasant or pleasing or agreeable in nature or appearance; - George Meredith
note: Two card defects that are not sense defects. (1) The headword is a comparative form — a lemmatisation miss; the definition is for 'nice' and carries no comparison. (2) The English ends with a dangling citation artifact, '; - George Meredith', a truncated WordNet example attribution that is being printed on the card. Same artifact appears on 'mad' in this batch, so it is a pipeline pattern, not a one-off. The Arabic ألطف correctly keeps the comparative the English lost.

en_definition: a push button at an outer door that gives a ringing or buzzing signal when pushed
expected: a device that makes a loud buzzing sound as a signal
note: WordNet sense 1 defines the push BUTTON at a door; the everyday referent is the sounding device (doorbell buzzer, quiz buzzer, the buzzer at the end of a game). Arabic طنّان means a buzzing/sounding device, i.e. it names the everyday sense the English definition does not describe — a mismatch in the direction of the better sense.

en_definition: take away to an undisclosed location against their will and usually in order to extract a ransom
note: Kidnapping is the everyday sense; the anatomical sense (draw a limb away from the body) is the obscure one and was correctly avoided. 'Usually in order to extract a ransom' over-specifies — plenty of abductions have no ransom — but it does not mislead. Arabic يَخْطِفّ is 'kidnaps/snatches'; it drops the ransom clause, and note the typo, a doubled shadda on the final ف (يَخْطِفّ for يَخْطِف).

en_definition: an upholstered seat for more than one person
note: Correct primary sense; أريكة is the standard equivalent.

en_definition: an awkward and inexperienced youth
expected: a young bear, lion, fox, or other wild animal
note: Textbook case of an obscure sense displacing the obvious one: 'an awkward and inexperienced youth' (as in 'cub reporter') is archaic outside that one collocation. Everyone means a young animal. The Arabic diverges twice over — هِجْرِس is a rare classical word for a fox cub/young animal, so it renders the animal sense the English definition does not give, and it is itself a word no modern learner will meet. Ordinary choices: شِبْل (lion cub), جَرْو (pup), or صَغِير + animal.

en_definition: in spite of everything; without regard to drawbacks
note: Right sense. Arabic بغض النظر is a truncated collocation — it normally requires عن plus a complement ('regardless of X'), so as a standalone adverb رغم كل شيء would render 'in spite of everything' better. The meaning is not wrong, just incomplete as a citation form.

en_definition: a fancy dock for small yachts and cabin cruisers
note: Right sense. 'Fancy' is an odd editorial word for a card — 'a harbour where small boats and yachts are kept' is neutral. Arabic مرسى اليخوت matches.

en_definition: a child of your son or daughter
note: Only sense the word has. حَفِيد matches (it leans masculine 'grandson'; حَفِيد/حَفِيدَة is the pair, but as a headword gloss it is fine).

en_definition: constituting the undiminished entirety; lacking nothing essential especially not damaged; - Bacon
note: Sense is correct and primary, but the English string is corrupt: the trailing "; - Bacon" is a leaked WordNet example attribution and is rendering on the card. "Whole and undamaged; with nothing missing" would be both clean and clearer than "constituting the undiminished entirety". The Arabic سليم is faithful to the undamaged sense and contains no such artifact, which confirms the leak is English-side only.

en_definition: now and then or here and there
note: 'Now and then' is correct; the trailing 'or here and there' is a spatial reading carried over from a shared synset and does not apply to this adverb — it should be trimmed. Arabic أحياناً translates the temporal part correctly and simply omits the spurious clause.

en_definition: a submerged ridge of rock or coral near the surface of the water
note: Commonest sense. Arabic شعاب is the usual word (as in الشعاب المرجانية) but is plural; a singular شِعْب مرجاني would match 'a ridge' more precisely.

en_definition: a son who has the same first name as his father
note: Correct for the name suffix. Arabic الابن الحامل لاسم أبيه is an accurate, if literal, rendering of the definition.

en_definition: a resentment strong enough to justify retaliation
note: Correct everyday sense (lasting resentment over a past wrong). Wording is clumsy: a grudge makes someone WANT revenge, it does not 'justify' it. ضغينة is the standard equivalent and matches.

en_definition: any federal law-enforcement officer
expected: past tense of 'feed' (gave food to); also, informally in the US, a federal agent
note: As a noun, 'a federal officer' is the main sense, so the POS tag makes it defensible. But a learner meeting the string 'fed' at rank 5208 will overwhelmingly meet the past tense of 'feed' — the rank almost certainly comes from that form. The card as written teaches a US-informal noun and leaves the learner unable to parse 'she fed the cat'. Arabic عميل فيدرالي faithfully renders the definition given.

en_definition: operating with minimal human intervention; independent of external control
note: Primary sense, correctly given. تلقائي matches.

en_definition: someone whose occupation is catching fish
note: Correct everyday sense (the animal sense, Martes pennanti, would have been the obscure trap and was avoided). Worth noting 'fisherman' is far commoner than 'fisher' in real use. Arabic صياد carries the sense but defaults to 'hunter' when it stands alone; صياد سمك would pin it to fish.

en_definition: refresh one's memory
expected: make fresh or restore energy again; also, reload a page so it shows the newest information
note: 'Refresh one's memory' is a real collocation but not the first sense at this rank, and the gloss is circular (defines refresh with refresh). Arabic جدد النشاط = 'renewed the energy', which translates the restore-energy sense, not the memory sense given in the English.

en_definition: a ghostly appearing figure
note: English is the right sense. Arabic سراب means 'mirage', a different referent from a ghostly figure; the definition calls for شبح or طيف.

en_definition: a branch of the Tai languages
expected: the Shan people of Myanmar, or their language — realistically this headword should not be a card at all
note: Accurate but a regional ethnonym/language-family label; an English learner at rank 5378 meets this only as corpus noise or a proper noun. Arabic شان is a bare transliteration of the name and conveys nothing of 'a branch of the Tai languages'.

en_definition: in an aggressive manner
expected: suddenly and by a large amount; also, in a harsh or critical way
note: By far the commonest use is the degree/abruptness sense (rose sharply, turned sharply); 'in an aggressive manner' captures only the harsh-speech sense. Arabic بحدة is a faithful translation of the definition as given.

en_definition: United States composer of works noted for their use of the American vernacular (1893-1969)
expected: a common English and Irish family name (Moore) — a proper noun, not a vocabulary item; the card is better removed than redefined
note: Classic lexical-database artefact: a surname whose entry resolves to one obscure individual (Douglas Moore, US composer). No learner meeting 'Moore' encounters that person. Arabic مور is the correct transliteration of the name, so the defect is entirely upstream — the Arabic carries none of the composer detail because the name is all there is to carry.

en_definition: a republic in southeastern Europe on the southern part of the Balkan peninsula; known for grapes and olives and olive oil
note: Only sense of the word; correct. WordNet-style encyclopedic padding ("known for grapes and olives and olive oil") is odd on a flashcard but does not change the sense. Arabic اليونان names the same referent rather than rendering the definition — on a recognition card it hands the learner the answer. Consider whether bare country names belong in a vocabulary deck at all.

en_definition: the Semitic language of the Arabs; spoken in a variety of dialects
note: The language is the sense learners meet. Arabic عَرَبِيّ standing alone reads most naturally as the adjective 'Arab/Arabic', or as a noun 'an Arab person'; اللُّغة العربية would name the language the definition actually describes. Same territory, imprecise landing.

en_definition: German tennis player who won seven women's singles titles at Wimbledon (born in 1969)
expected: a paragraph (journalism slang) — or drop the card: this headword is a surname, not an English word
note: This is a WordNet proper-noun entry for Steffi Graf, not a sense of a lowercase English word. A learner cannot learn any vocabulary from it, and the frequency rank is almost certainly counting the surname plus unrelated tokens. The card should be removed rather than redefined; if kept, the only lexical sense is the newsroom clipping of 'paragraph'. Arabic غراف is a transliteration of the name, which is the right treatment for a proper noun, so the translation is not the defect here.

en_definition: hit with a pinging noise
expected: to send someone a short message or alert; also to make a short, high ringing sound
note: The transitive 'hit with a pinging noise' (WordNet's 'the bugs pinged the lampshade') is close to unused. At rank 5562 in any modern corpus the hits are 'ping me when you're done' and network/sonar pings. A learner would take away a usage they will never produce. The Arabic يصدر صوت رنين says 'emits a ringing sound' — intransitive, dropping the 'hit with' that is the whole point of the English definition.

en_definition: interrupt temporarily an activity before continuing
note: Standard everyday sense. The ar column throughout this batch is a one-word headword gloss, not a rendering of the definition sentence; تَوَقُّف is the verbal noun (a stop/halt) for a verb entry, so the form is nominal and 'temporarily / before continuing' is lost, but the concept matches. تَوَقَّفَ مُؤَقَّتاً would fit the verb entry better.

en_definition: usually brightly colored zygodactyl tropical birds with short hooked beaks and the ability to mimic sounds
note: Right sense, but the wording is needlessly technical — 'zygodactyl' is opaque to a learner at rank 5591 and adds nothing to recognition. Sense choice is correct, so this is a wording issue, not a sense issue. ببغاء matches.

en_definition: provide commentary for a film, for example
expected: to tell a story, or describe events in the order they happened
note: The film/voice-over sense is real and reasonably common, but it is a specialisation of the everyday 'tell a story' sense, and the hedge 'for a film, for example' makes a weak card. The Arabic حَكَى means to tell or recount a story — that is the sense the definition does NOT give, so English and Arabic point at different senses here.

en_definition: strike against forcefully
note: For the verb this is the commonest sense (beat repeatedly, strike hard). Note the far commoner noun senses (cake batter, baseball batter) live on other cards. يضرب بعنف matches.

en_definition: believed or reputed to be the case
note: Right sense. It slightly undersells the sceptical nuance — 'supposedly' usually implies the speaker doubts it — which 'believed or reputed to be the case' leaves implicit. يُفترض أنه matches the definition as written and carries a similar hedge.

en_definition: an act of deliberate betrayal
note: Correct sense but wholly circular — 'an act of deliberate betrayal' defines the headword with the headword, so it conveys nothing to a learner. Suggested rewrite: 'the act of breaking the trust of someone who trusted you'. خيانة is the right equivalent.

en_definition: on or starting from the wearer's right
note: This heraldic sense is essentially the word's only adjectival sense, so nothing commoner is being displaced — the definition is not the defect. The word is: 'dexter' outside heraldry is a given name and a cattle breed, which is almost certainly what pushed it to rank 5668. Worth checking whether it belongs in the list at all. Arabic أيمن ('right-hand, right') carries the core but drops 'the wearer's', losing the heraldic point.

en_definition: spaghetti served with a tomato sauce
expected: long thin strings of pasta
note: Defines the dish (pasta in tomato sauce) rather than the pasta itself, and is circular — the headword appears in its own definition. Arabic معكرونة is generic pasta/macaroni and drops the tomato-sauce element that is the whole point of the English gloss.

en_definition: an organization formed by merging several groups or parties
note: Covers the everyday sense (a union of groups, states or associations), though 'merging' is slightly off — a federation is an association, not a merger. اتحادية is defensible (as in الاتحادية الروسية); plain اتحاد would be the more neutral gloss.

en_definition: any man who serves as a sponsor for a child at baptism
note: The baptismal sponsor is the literal and still-primary sense; the mafia-boss sense is the derived one. عَرَّاب carries both in Arabic, same as English.

en_definition: a port in southern Lebanon on the Mediterranean Sea; formerly a major Phoenician seaport famous for silks
expected: the thick rubber ring fitted around a wheel, usually filled with air
note: The definition describes the proper noun Tyre, the Phoenician city in Lebanon — a different word from the common noun 'tyre' that earns rank 5720 as the British spelling of 'tire'. The Arabic إِطَار is correct for the word (the rubber tyre) and therefore contradicts the English definition, which is the clearest possible signal that the English entry grabbed the wrong homograph.

en_definition: United States rock singer who was one of the first to popularize rock'n'roll music (1925-1981)
expected: an English given name and surname (drop from the deck — it is a proper noun, not vocabulary)
note: This is WordNet's proper-noun entry for Bill Haley. Whatever drives 'haley' to rank 5834 is the given name and surname, not the 1950s rock singer, and no learner will recognise or need this. Recommend removal rather than redefinition. The Arabic هالي is a bare transliteration of the name and conveys none of the definition's content.

en_definition: bulbous herb of southern Europe widely naturalized; bulb breaks up into separate strong-flavored cloves
expected: a strong-smelling bulb made up of small cloves, used in cooking
note: This is the botanical plant sense; the everyday referent is the food. A learner can still get there via 'strong-flavored cloves', so it is not a trap, but 'bulbous herb of southern Europe widely naturalized' is a field-guide entry, not a flashcard. ثوم is the correct referent.

en_definition: a college or university building containing living quarters for students
note: Primary sense; note that in American use 'dorm' is also the room itself, not only the building. Arabic سكن طلابي ('student housing') is faithful, shifting building to accommodation, which is the idiomatic equivalent.

en_definition: any of numerous small celestial bodies composed of rock and metal that move around the sun (mainly between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter)
note: Only sense; correct. كويكب is the standard equivalent.

en_definition: general who commanded the Carthaginian army in the second Punic War; crossed the Alps and defeated the Romans but was recalled to defend Carthage and was defeated (247-182 BC)
note: Definition matches the canonical referent, so not wrong, but this is a proper noun with an encyclopedic dictionary entry and does not belong in a vocabulary deck at all — nothing here is learnable English vocabulary, and for many learners the first Hannibal met today is fictional. Arabic هانيبال is just the name transliterated and translates none of the definition.

en_definition: migration into a place (especially migration to a country of which you are not a native in order to settle there)
note: Correct sense including the directional 'into'. Arabic هِجْرَة is the general word for migration/emigration and does not by itself encode the inbound direction the parenthetical stresses; هِجْرَة وَافِدَة is the precise term. Faithful to the definition's headline, imprecise on its qualifier.

en_definition: relatively permanent disorder of the mind
note: Gives madness, which is the everyday sense; the legal-defence sense is the secondary one and is correctly not used here. جُنُون matches.

en_definition: find fault with; express criticism of; point out real or perceived flaws
note: Commonest everyday sense, clearly worded. اِنْتَقَدَ is the standard equivalent and carries the same find-fault meaning.

en_definition: hypersensitivity reaction to a particular allergen; symptoms can vary greatly in intensity
note: Correct everyday sense. Minor wording gripe only: the gloss defines 'allergy' with 'allergen', which is circular for a learner, and 'hypersensitivity reaction' is clinical register. Arabic أَرَجِيَّة is a genuine but bookish term; حساسية is the word an Arabic speaker would actually use.

en_definition: (Arthurian legend) the magician who acted as King Arthur's advisor
note: The Arthurian magician is what an ordinary speaker means by Merlin, so the English sense choice is defensible — but two things are off. It is a proper name on a common-noun vocabulary card, which is worth questioning upstream, and the Arabic يؤيؤ is the bird (the small falcon Falco columbarius), i.e. the OTHER sense of the headword entirely. English and Arabic on this card teach two unrelated things.

en_definition: take temporary possession of as a security, by legal authority
expected: to take something away from someone officially, usually as a punishment
note: 'Take temporary possession of as a security, by legal authority' is the legal attachment/sequestration sense (WordNet's shared gloss with impound/sequester). Everyday confiscation is a penalty and is not temporary, so the card teaches a wrong entailment. Arabic صادر is the right verb for the everyday sense and does not contradict the English — the defect is upstream.

en_definition: moderate in type or degree or effect or force; far from extreme
note: Commonest sense (mild weather, a mild cold). معتدل matches 'moderate'.

en_definition: completely out of control
expected: having escaped or fled; also, out of control
note: 'Completely out of control' is a real and common adjective sense (runaway inflation, runaway train), but the escape sense (a runaway child, runaway bride) is what most speakers reach for first. Borderline — the card is not misleading, just not the first sense. Arabic جامح (unruly, unrestrained) matches the definition as given well.

en_definition: an Italian poet famous for writing the Divine Comedy that describes a journey through Hell and purgatory and paradise guided by Virgil and his idealized Beatrice (1265-1321)
note: Accurate, and the poet is the dominant referent for the name, so the sense is right. Two separate issues: the definition is far too long for a card that has to be recognised at a glance, and a proper noun in a vocabulary deck is a deck-composition question rather than a definition one. Arabic is a bare transliteration of the name with none of the definition's content — same pattern as omega and perry, which together look like proper-noun entries systematically shipping a transliterated headword in place of a translated definition.

en_definition: the act of examining resemblances
note: Correct main sense, though 'examining resemblances' is narrow — comparison examines differences as well; 'the act of examining how two things are alike or different' would be truer. مقارنة is the exact equivalent.

en_definition: a road leading up to a private house
note: Exactly the everyday sense. Arabic ممر السيارات renders it well.

en_definition: the process of becoming warmer; a rising temperature
expected: the system that keeps a building warm (central heating); also the act of making something warm
note: As a noun, 'heating' in ordinary use is the house system you turn on, not the abstract process of a temperature rising — that reading belongs more to 'warming'. Interestingly the Arabic تَدْفِئَة gives exactly the space-heating sense, i.e. the better sense, which means it does not match the English definition as written (that would be ارتفاع الحرارة / تسخين). Fix the English and the Arabic becomes right.

en_definition: (of something seen or heard) clearly defined
expected: firm and fresh so that it breaks easily (a crisp apple, crisp bacon); also (of air) cold and fresh
note: 'Clearly defined' (crisp image, crisp sound) is a real and current sense, but the texture sense — crisp food — is what an ordinary speaker means first, with crisp weather second. واضح is a fair rendering of 'clearly defined' as given, so the Arabic is not the defect here.

en_definition: of or relating to or characteristic of Denmark or the Danes or their language
note: Standard demonym adjective. Arabic دنماركي is exact. (The pastry sense is a noun and correctly not used here.)

en_definition: watch and direct
note: Commonest sense, plainly worded. يشرف matches.

en_definition: (physics) a brief event in which two or more bodies come together
expected: a crash; when two moving things hit each other
note: The "(physics)" tag and "come together" give the technical sense; the everyday sense is a crash, with impact and usually damage. A learner would half-recognise it but learn the wrong register. Arabic تصادم carries the general collision sense and matches the content. Diacritic bug: تَصَادُّم has a shadda on the dal; it should be تَصَادُم.

en_definition: an (apparently) flying object whose nature is unknown; especially those considered to have extraterrestrial origins
note: English sense is correct, if wordy. Arabic يُو أَف أَو is a phonetic spelling-out of the three English letters, not a translation — it carries none of the definition's content. Expected Arabic: جسم طائر مجهول.

en_definition: known widely and usually unfavorably
note: English is the everyday sense (famous for something bad). The Arabic مشنوع means 'abominable / reviled' (root ش-ن-ع, or a confusion with مَشْنُوء 'detested') — it carries the badness but not the 'widely known' element the definition leads with, so it says something the definition does not. سَيِّئ السُّمْعَة or مَشْهُور بِالسُّوء is the match.

en_definition: an arrangement of flowers that is usually given as a present
note: Commonest sense, plainly worded. باقة is the standard equivalent, but standing alone it also reads as 'bundle/package' (باقة إنترنت). باقة زهور would remove the ambiguity and match 'arrangement of flowers' exactly; marking faithful rather than diverging because باقة is the dictionary equivalent of bouquet.

en_definition: act of ascertaining or fixing the value or worth of
note: "Fixing the value or worth of" leans towards appraisal, but it is the ordinary assessment sense a learner meets (performance evaluation, evaluation of results). تَقْيِيم is the standard term and matches.

en_definition: the classification of someone or something with respect to its worth
note: Right sense (an evaluation/judgement of worth), but 'the classification of someone or something with respect to its worth' is opaque; 'a judgement about how good, valuable or serious something is' would be recognisable. تَقْدِير (estimation, appraisal) tracks the definition as written.

en_definition: a state of abeyance or suspended business
expected: (of a court, parliament or school) to stop work for a break
note: POS is verb but the gloss is a noun gloss ('a state of abeyance or suspended business') — a learner cannot produce the verb from it. The noun senses a learner actually meets are the school break and the alcove in a wall. Arabic عطلة = 'holiday/day off', which is not 'a state of abeyance or suspended business' (توقف/تعليق الجلسات).

en_definition: a preschool for children age 4 to 6 to prepare them for primary school
note: Correct, though 'age 4 to 6' is a US-specific detail that is untrue in several systems. رَوْضَة is the ordinary word.

en_definition: to cause someone to lose clear vision, especially from intense light
note: The literal light sense is primary and correctly stated; the figurative 'impress greatly' sense is arguably as common and could be appended. Arabic يبهر spans both, matching well.

en_definition: a datum that can be represented numerically
note: 'A number that represents a fact' is what an ordinary speaker means ('a shocking statistic'). Arabic اِحْصَائِيَّة is the standard equivalent.

en_definition: a poor ability to understand or to profit from experience
note: Captures the trait sense, which is the commonest; misses the count sense (a stupid act, 'one of his stupidities') but that is the lesser one. Arabic غباء is exact.

en_definition: make stable and keep from fluctuating or put into an equilibrium
note: Commonest sense, clearly stated. Arabic يثبت matches.

en_definition: a device that shreds documents (usually in order to prevent the wrong people from reading them)
note: Commonest sense and the parenthetical explains why the object exists. آلة تمزيق الورق is an accurate and idiomatic rendering.

en_definition: the top of a (usually flat) roof
note: Right sense, but the definition is circular — it explains 'rooftop' with 'roof', so a learner who does not know 'roof' gets nothing. Sense verdict is primary; the wording is a separate card-quality issue. سطح is the natural Arabic equivalent.

en_definition: anesthesia of the lower half of the body; caused by injury to the spinal cord or by injecting an anesthetic beneath the arachnoid membrane that surrounds the spinal cord
expected: relating to the spine or backbone (as in spinal cord, spinal injury)
note: This is the medical noun 'a spinal' = spinal anaesthetic, plus a garbled clause about spinal-cord injury. A learner meets 'spinal' as the adjective in 'spinal cord'. The Arabic فِقْرِيّ means 'vertebral/spinal (adj)' — it renders the word's ordinary adjective sense, not the anaesthesia definition on the card, so English and Arabic sides of this card disagree with each other.

en_definition: terms of abuse for a masturbator
expected: British vulgar slang: a contemptible or stupid person
note: The literal sense is real but almost never what is meant — in actual use this is an all-purpose insult. 'Terms of abuse for' half-acknowledges that while still anchoring on the literal reading. The Arabic أحمق ('fool') renders the idiomatic insult, not the English as given, so it diverges — but it is the better gloss of the two. Separately: consider whether a vulgar item belongs on a card at all.

en_definition: using speech rather than writing
note: English gives the speech sense, which is the one a learner meets (oral exam, oral agreement). Arabic فموي means 'of the mouth' — the other sense entirely. Should be شفهي / شفوي.

en_definition: a car in which policemen cruise the streets; equipped with radiotelephonic communications to headquarters
expected: a police patrol car; also a warship, or a large motorboat
note: The police-car sense is common in US English but competes with the warship and cabin-cruiser senses, and the trailing clause 'equipped with radiotelephonic communications to headquarters' is antiquated filler. Verdict held at secondary with low confidence because the primary sense is genuinely region-dependent. The Arabic طَرَّاد is the naval cruiser — a different sense from the one the English defines.

en_definition: the ending of a series or sequence; --Revelation
expected: the last letter of the Greek alphabet (Ω); also, the very end of something
note: The figurative 'the alpha and the omega' sense has displaced the literal one. A learner meeting omega meets a Greek letter — in maths, physics, brand names, omega-3 — before they meet Revelation. Also, '--Revelation' is a leaked source citation from the lexical database and should not be on a card at all. The Arabic is a bare transliteration of the headword and carries none of the definition's content.

en_definition: a social club for male undergraduates
note: In current usage the US college society is the commonest sense, so the definition is a reasonable pick — but it is strongly American, and the 'brotherhood / group sharing a profession or interest' sense ('the medical fraternity') is what a learner is more likely to meet in British or international text. Worth a second sense rather than a correction. Arabic أخوية طلابية ('student fraternity') tracks the definition, dropping only 'male'.

en_definition: tread or stomp heavily or roughly
note: Everyday sense, plainly worded. Arabic يدوس is the ordinary verb for treading/trampling and matches the definition.

en_definition: no longer in existence; lost or especially having died out leaving no living representatives
note: Commonest sense, clearly worded. منقرض is exact.

en_definition: cause to be firmly attached
note: Commonest sense, fine at this rank. Arabic يثبت (yuthabbit) reads correctly as 'secures/fastens'; it is unvocalised where neighbouring entries are vowelled, which matters because bare يثبت can also be read yathbutu ('is firm', intransitive) — worth a shadda/damma from the vowelling pass.

en_definition: a group of people who adhere to a common faith and habitually attend a given church
note: The church-attending group is the everyday sense. Arabic جَمَاعَة is a legitimate gloss and carries the religious-assembly reading in Arabic (as in صلاة الجماعة), though it is broader than the English and drops 'church' and 'common faith'; a learner reading only the Arabic would get 'group' and miss the religious specificity.

en_definition: just below the level of consciousness
note: Sense is right for the adjective. The Arabic اللاوعي is the definite NOUN ('the subconscious'), not an adjective, so it glosses the concept rather than the property the card declares (adj); an adjectival لاشعوري / لاواعٍ would match the POS.

en_definition: a building occupied by a state legislature
note: Correct and essentially the only sense of this spelling. Arabic مبنى الكابيتول names one specific building (the US Capitol in Washington) rather than translating the general class 'a building occupied by a state legislature' — a proper noun standing in for a definition. مبنى الهيئة التشريعية للولاية would be faithful.

en_definition: any plant of the genus Lupinus; bearing erect spikes of usually purplish-blue flowers
note: The garden plant is the only sense in ordinary use, and the flower-spike description is what identifies it. Arabic ترمس is the same plant, though in Arabic it most often evokes the edible lupin beans rather than the ornamental flower — same referent, different salient image.

en_definition: place in a line or arrange so as to be parallel or straight
note: Commonest sense; يُحاذي matches.

en_definition: the path followed by an object moving through space
note: Core sense, stated plainly. مَسَار matches.

en_definition: a record in which commercial accounts are recorded
note: Commonest sense. دفتر حسابات is exact.

en_definition: an advocate of anarchism
note: Correct and standard; mildly circular on 'anarchism', but recoverable. Arabic فوضوي is the normal equivalent.

en_definition: extramarital sex that willfully and maliciously interferes with marriage relations
note: Right sense, but the legalistic padding ("willfully and maliciously interferes with marriage relations") is noise for a learner; plain wording would be "sex between a married person and someone other than their spouse". Arabic خِيانة زَوْجِيَّة conveys the sense, dropping the legal wording.

en_definition: someone who has supervisory duties at a summer camp
expected: someone trained to give advice and support to people with personal problems; an adviser
note: The summer-camp-supervisor sense is a US-specific, vanishingly narrow reading displacing the obvious one (therapist/adviser; in some jurisdictions a lawyer). Notably the Arabic مرشد translates the CORRECT everyday sense (guide/counsellor), not the camp-supervisor definition on the card — so the two layers disagree, and the English is the one that is wrong.

en_definition: the outside boundary or surface of something
expected: the decorative border of hanging threads on cloth; also the outer edge or margin of something
note: This is WordNet's 'periphery/outskirt' gloss; 'or surface' is simply wrong for fringe. The edge/margin sense is real (fringe group, on the fringes) but the trim-on-cloth sense is what most speakers picture first. The Arabic هُدْب means the fringe/tassel of a garment (also eyelash) — i.e. the sense the English definition did NOT give, so the two sides of the card disagree.

en_definition: of the relatively near future
note: Primary and only real sense. قادم matches. Minor inconsistency: no diacritics here while most entries in the batch are vowelled.

en_definition: normal use of the faculty of vision
note: Right sense, clumsily worded: 'normal use of the faculty of vision' is harder to decode than the word itself, and 'normal' wrongly implies poor eyesight is not eyesight. 'The ability to see' is what belongs on the card. Arabic بَصَر matches.

en_definition: any of various tall and stout herbs of the genus Angelica having pinnately compound leaves and small white or greenish flowers in compound umbels
note: Right sense (the plant), but the wording is lifted botanical description — 'pinnately compound leaves', 'compound umbels' are unreadable on a flashcard. A learner would recognise it from 'a tall plant with clusters of small greenish-white flowers, used in cooking'. Arabic حشيشة الملاك is the correct plant name.

en_definition: an unpleasant smell
note: 'An unpleasant smell' is the main noun sense, so nothing obscure has displaced anything — but flagging it as British informal would help, since a learner will rarely meet it and may otherwise try to use it in neutral registers. The rank itself is suspect: much of it likely comes from 'ping pong' and the game name rather than the smell. Arabic رائحة كريهة translates the definition exactly.

en_definition: a character set that includes letters and is used to write a language
note: Correct and the only sense that matters. 'Character set' is faintly computational phrasing for a word every learner already half-knows; 'the set of letters used to write a language' would be plainer. Arabic حُرُوف هِجَاء is the standard term.

en_definition: young bull
note: 'young bull' is the standard American reading and not obscure. Worth knowing that British and Indian English usually mean a castrated ox (bullock cart), so the card is slightly US-shaped. Arabic عجل is 'calf' — right animal, loses the male/young-bull specificity rather than contradicting it.

en_definition: not suited to your comfort, purpose or needs
note: Right sense, plainly worded. غير مناسب renders 'not suited' accurately, though it drops the 'to your comfort, purpose or needs' qualifier and so reads slightly broader (closer to 'unsuitable'); غير ملائم would be tighter.

en_definition: a fee charged in advance to retain the services of someone
note: Fee sense is the standard written sense and defensible at this rank, though for many everyday speakers 'retainer' first evokes the dental appliance. Arabic عربون is a deposit/earnest money against a purchase, not a fee paid to secure someone's services; أتعاب مقدمة would translate the definition given.

en_definition: without shoes
note: 'without shoes' is the whole meaning. حَافٍ is exact.

en_definition: a married woman (usually middle-aged with children) who is staid and dignified
expected: an older married woman; also a woman in charge of nursing or domestic arrangements in a hospital, school or prison
note: The 'staid, dignified married woman' sense is real but competes with the institutional sense (hospital/prison/school matron) that a learner is likelier to meet, and with 'matron of honor'. Not obscure, so not rare — just the second thing most people think of. Arabic compresses to 'a dignified lady' and drops 'married', 'middle-aged' and 'with children', i.e. every element that narrows the definition; omission rather than contradiction.
